summary: Describes how Ethernet VPN can support Virtual Private Wire Service in MPLS/IP networks. It provides single-active and all-active multihoming with flow-based load balancing, removes the need for pseudowire signaling, and gives fast protection convergence.

plainLanguage.summary: EVPN already tells a provider's routers which customer sites are attached where, and which label to use to reach each one. RFC 8214 reuses that machinery for a service that connects exactly two customer sites, so no separate pseudowire signalling is needed. The result is faster failover and the option to spread traffic over several provider routers at once.

subtitle: How Ethernet VPN carries point-to-point wire services over MPLS/IP without pseudowire signalling.

tldr.problem: A point-to-point Ethernet service between two customer sites normally needs its own pseudowire signalling, and the traditional way of providing it offers only single-active redundancy, with backup paths that never carry traffic.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8214 signals the service with the same per-EVI Ethernet auto-discovery routes that EVPN already uses, with the service instance identifier placed in the Ethernet Tag field and the MPLS label identifying the far end. A new Layer 2 Attributes extended community carries the primary, backup and control-word flags and the layer 2 MTU.
tldr.outcome: Both single-active and all-active multihoming become available, traffic can be balanced across the provider edges attached to one customer, and failover is a single route withdrawal. The document is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: EVPN instance rule
facts.value: No mix with multipoint EVPN services

today: RFC 8214 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2017, and it has not been obsoleted. It defines the EVPN-VPWS service on top of the EVPN control plane specified in RFC 7432.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document describes how EVPN can be used to support VPWS in MPLS and IP networks. The use of EVPN mechanisms for VPWS brings the benefits of EVPN to point-to-point services, including single-active redundancy as well as all-active redundancy with flow-based load-balancing. It also eliminates the need for the traditional way of pseudowire signalling for point-to-point Ethernet services.

RFC 7432 provides the ability to forward customer traffic to and from a given customer Attachment Circuit without any MAC lookup. That capability suits point-to-point services, also known as VPWS services. The Metro Ethernet Forum defines the Ethernet Virtual Private Line service as a point-to-point service between a pair of Attachment Circuits designated by VLANs, and the Ethernet Private Line service, in which all traffic flows between a single pair of ports. EVPL can be considered a VPWS with only two Attachment Circuits. In delivering an EVPL service, the traffic-forwarding capability of EVPN is based on the exchange of a pair of Ethernet Auto-Discovery routes, whereas for more general VPWS as defined in RFC 4664 it is based on the exchange of a group of Ethernet auto-discovery routes, one per Attachment Circuit or Ethernet Segment. In a VPWS service, traffic from an originating Ethernet Segment can be forwarded only to a single destination Ethernet Segment, so no MAC lookup is needed, and the MPLS label associated with the per-EVPN-instance Ethernet auto-discovery route can be used to forward user traffic to the destination Attachment Circuit.

For both EPL and EVPL services, a specific VPWS service instance is identified by a pair of per-EVPN-instance Ethernet auto-discovery routes that together identify the endpoints of the instance. In the control plane the service instance is identified using the VPWS service instance identifiers advertised by each Provider Edge node; in the data plane the value of the MPLS label advertised by one PE is used by the other PE to send traffic for that instance. As with the Ethernet Tag in standard EVPN, the VPWS service instance identifier is unique within an EVPN instance.

For EVPN routes, the Ethernet Tag IDs are set to zero for port-based, VLAN-based and VLAN bundle interface modes, and to non-zero values for VLAN-aware bundle mode. For EVPN-VPWS, the Ethernet Tag ID in the Ethernet auto-discovery route must be set to a non-zero value for all four service interface types.

In terms of route advertisement and MPLS label lookup behaviour, EVPN-VPWS resembles the VLAN-aware bundle mode of RFC 7432, in that when a PE advertises a per-EVPN-instance Ethernet auto-discovery route, the VPWS service instance serves as a 32-bit normalized Ethernet Tag ID. The value of the MPLS label in that route represents both the EVPN instance and the VPWS service instance, so that upon receiving an MPLS-encapsulated packet the disposition PE can identify the egress Attachment Circuit from the MPLS label and then perform any required tag translation. For the EVPL service, the Ethernet frames transported over an MPLS or IP network should remain tagged with the originating VLAN ID, and any VLAN ID translation must be performed at the disposition PE. For the EPL service, the frames are transported as they are and the tags are not altered.

The MPLS label value in the Ethernet auto-discovery route can be set to the VXLAN Network Identifier for VXLAN encapsulation as per RFC 7348, and that identifier has a local scope per PE and may also be equal to the VPWS service instance identifier. The EVPN-VPWS techniques defined here have no dependency on the tunnelling technology. The Ethernet Segment Identifier encoded in the per-EVPN-instance route is not used to identify the service, but it can be used for flow-based load-balancing and mass withdraw functions as per the RFC 7432 baseline. As with standard EVPN, the per-Ethernet-Segment auto-discovery route is used for fast convergence upon link or node failure, for auto-discovery of the PEs attached to a given multihomed customer edge, and to synchronize state between them.
sections.plainLanguage: A point-to-point service has exactly two ends, so there is never a question of which of several sites to send a frame to. EVPN-VPWS puts the identifier of that service into the field EVPN already uses to name a VLAN, and uses the advertised label to reach the far end. Because the signalling is ordinary EVPN, the same redundancy models work as they do for any other EVPN service.

sections.title: Service Interfaces
sections.content:
With the VLAN-based service interface, a VPWS instance identifier corresponds to a single VLAN on a specific interface, so there is a one-to-one mapping between a VLAN ID on that interface and the VPWS service instance identifier. The PE provides the cross-connect functionality between an MPLS Label Switched Path identified by the VPWS service instance identifier and a specific port and VLAN. If the VLAN is represented by different VLAN IDs on different PEs and different Ethernet Segments, each PE needs to perform VLAN ID translation for frames destined to its Ethernet Segment. In such scenarios the frames transported over the network should remain tagged with the originating VLAN ID, and a VLAN ID translation must be supported in the data path and must be performed on the disposition PE.

With the VLAN bundle service interface, a VPWS service instance identifier corresponds to multiple VLANs on a specific interface. The PE provides the cross-connect functionality between the MPLS label identified by the VPWS service instance identifier and a group of VLANs on a specific interface. For this service interface each VLAN is presented by a single VLAN ID, which means no VLAN translation is allowed, and the receiving PE can direct traffic, on the EVPN label alone, to a specific port. The transmitting PE can cross-connect traffic from a group of VLANs on a specific port to the MPLS label, and the MPLS-encapsulated frames must remain tagged with the originating VLAN ID.

The port-based service interface is a special case of the VLAN bundle service interface, where all of the VLANs on the port are mapped to the same VPWS service instance identifier, and the procedures are identical.

The VLAN-aware bundle service interface is not used in EVPN-VPWS. In EVPN it maps to a VLAN-based service interface, and in EVPN-VPWS the same is true, so defining data-plane and control-plane behaviour for it would give the same result as the VLAN-based service.
sections.plainLanguage: Three ways of attaching the service to the customer are defined. One VLAN on one port, a group of VLANs on one port, or every VLAN on a port. The first allows the VLAN number to differ at the two ends and the PE translates it; the other two do not, because the label alone must be enough to pick the right port.

sections.title: BGP Extensions
sections.content:
The document specifies the use of the per-EVPN-instance Ethernet auto-discovery route to signal VPWS services. The Ethernet Segment Identifier field is set to the customer Ethernet Segment, and the 32-bit Ethernet Tag ID field must be set to the VPWS service instance identifier value. That value may be set to a 24-bit value, and when a 24-bit value is used it must be right-aligned. For both EPL and EVPL services using a given VPWS service instance, the pair of PEs instantiating that instance will each advertise a per-EVPN-instance Ethernet auto-discovery route with its VPWS service instance identifier, and will each be configured with the other PE's identifier. When each PE has received the other PE's route, the VPWS service instance is instantiated. The same VPWS service instance identifier may be configured on both PEs.

The Route Target extended community with which the per-EVPN-instance route is tagged identifies the EVPN instance in which the VPWS service instance is configured. It is the operator's choice how many and which VPWS service instances are configured in a given EVPN instance. However, a given EVPN instance must not be configured with both VPWS service instances and standard EVPN multipoint services.

A new extended community is defined to be included with the per-EVPN-instance Ethernet auto-discovery routes, and this attribute is mandatory if multihoming is enabled. It is eight octets long: a two-octet Type and Sub-Type field with type 0x06 and sub-type 0x04, a two-octet Control Flags field, a two-octet L2 MTU field, and two reserved octets. The control flags are a two-octet field in which the remaining bits must be set to zero when sending and must be ignored when receiving. The P flag, if set to 1 in multihoming single-active scenarios, indicates that the advertising PE is the primary PE, and must be set to 1 by all active PEs in multihoming all-active scenarios. The B flag, if set to 1 in multihoming single-active scenarios, indicates that the advertising PE is the backup PE. The C flag, if set to 1, means a control word must be present when sending EVPN packets to this PE, and it is recommended that the control word be included in the absence of an entropy label.

The L2 MTU is a two-octet value indicating the MTU in bytes. A received L2 MTU of zero means that no MTU checking against the local MTU is needed. A received non-zero MTU must be checked against the local MTU, and if there is a mismatch the local PE must not add the remote PE as the EVPN destination for the corresponding VPWS service instance. The usage of the per-Ethernet-Segment auto-discovery route is unchanged from RFC 7432: the single-active bit in the flags of the ESI Label extended community indicates whether single-active or all-active redundancy is used for that Ethernet Segment.
sections.plainLanguage: Each service instance is announced with an ordinary EVPN route whose Ethernet Tag field holds the instance number, and the label in that route is the label to send traffic to. A new eight-octet extended community travels with the route. Three of its flag bits say whether this PE is the primary, the backup, or whether packets to it must carry a control word, and a two-octet field carries the largest frame the far end can take.

sections.title: Operation
sections.content:
The deployment model has a customer edge device at each end of the service, each attached to two provider edges, with autonomous system border routers between the provider edges. iBGP sessions are established between PE1, PE2, ASBR1 and ASBR3, possibly via a BGP route reflector, and similarly among PE3, PE4, ASBR2 and ASBR4. eBGP sessions are established among the ASBRs. All PEs and ASBRs are enabled for the EVPN Subsequent Address Family Identifier and exchange per-EVPN-instance Ethernet auto-discovery routes, one route per VPWS service instance. For inter-AS option B, the ASBRs re-advertise these routes with the NEXT_HOP attribute set to their own IP addresses.

The link between the customer edge and the PE is either a customer-tagged or service-tagged interface that can carry a single VLAN tag or two nested VLAN tags, configured as a trunk with multiple VLANs, one per VPWS service instance. The VLAN ID used by the customer at either end to identify a service instance may be different, and EVPN does not perform that translation between the two values. The MPLS label identifies the service instance, and if translation is needed it should be done by the Ethernet interface for each service.

For a single-homed customer edge, in an advertised per-EVPN-instance route the Ethernet Segment Identifier field is set to zero and the Ethernet Tag ID is set to the VPWS service instance identifier. For a multihomed customer edge, the Ethernet Segment Identifier field is set to the customer's ESI and the Ethernet Tag ID is set to the VPWS service instance identifier, which must have the same value on all PEs attached to that Ethernet Segment. This allows an ingress PE in a multihoming all-active scenario to perform flow-based load-balancing of traffic flows to all of the PEs attached to that segment. In all cases traffic follows the transport paths, which may be asymmetric.

Either the VPWS service instance identifier encoded in the Ethernet Tag ID must be unique across all autonomous systems, or an ASBR needs to perform a translation when the route is re-advertised from one AS to the other. A per-Ethernet-Segment auto-discovery route can be used for mass withdraw, to withdraw all the per-EVPN-instance routes associated with the multihomed site on a given PE.

In a multihoming all-active scenario there is no Designated Forwarder election, and all the PEs in the segment that are active and ready to forward traffic set the P flag. A remote PE does per-flow load-balancing to the PEs that set the P flag for the same Ethernet Tag and ESI. The B flag should not be set in the all-active scenario and must be ignored by receivers if set. In a multihoming single-active scenario for a given VPWS service instance, the Designated Forwarder election should result in the primary-elected PE advertising the P flag set and the B flag clear, the backup-elected PE advertising the P flag clear and the B flag set, and the other PEs in the same segment signalling both clear. When the primary fails, it withdraws the associated Ethernet auto-discovery routes for the service instance, and the remote PE then sends traffic to the backup PE. Designated Forwarder re-election happens between the PEs in the same segment, and the newly elected primary and backup signal the flags as described. A remote PE should receive the P flag set from only one primary PE and the B flag set from only one backup PE, but during transients it selects the last advertising PE. A remote PE must receive the P flag set from at least one PE before forwarding traffic. If a network uses entropy labels, the C flag must not be set and the control word must not be used when sending EVPN-encapsulated packets over a point-to-point LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: Each end of the service advertises its own route and is configured with the other end's identifier, so the service comes into being when both sides have heard from the other. When a customer site is connected to more than one provider router, the flag bits tell the far end which of them is active, and the far end can spread traffic over all of them if the site is set to all-active.

sections.title: EVPN Compared with PW Signalling
sections.content:
In EVPN, service endpoint discovery and label signalling are done concurrently using BGP, whereas with VPWS based on RFC 4448, label signalling is done via LDP and service endpoint discovery is either through manual provisioning or through BGP.

In existing implementations of VPWS using pseudowires, redundancy is limited to single-active mode, while with EVPN implementations of VPWS, both single-active and all-active redundancy modes can be supported. In existing implementations with pseudowires, backup pseudowires are not used to carry traffic, while with EVPN traffic can be load-balanced among the different PEs multihomed to a single customer edge.

Upon link or node failure, EVPN can trigger failover with the withdrawal of a single BGP route per EVPL service, or multiple EVPL services, whereas with VPWS pseudowire redundancy the failover sequence requires the exchange of two control-plane messages: one to deactivate the group of primary pseudowires and a second to activate the group of backup pseudowires associated with the access link.

Finally, EVPN may employ data-plane egress link protection mechanisms not available in VPWS. This can be done by the primary PE, on a local Attachment Circuit going down, using the label advertised in the per-EVPN-instance route by the backup PE to encapsulate the traffic and direct it to the backup PE.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way needed two signalling systems: one to find the far end and another to set up the label. EVPN does both with BGP. The old way also only had one working path, with a spare that stood by unused, and switching to it took two messages. EVPN withdraws a route and traffic moves, and the spare path can carry traffic alongside the primary.

sections.title: Failure Scenarios
sections.content:
On a link or port failure between the customer edge and the PE, for both single-homed and multihomed customer edges, unlike RFC 7432 the PE must withdraw all the associated Ethernet auto-discovery routes for the VPWS service instances on the failed port or link.

For single-homed customer edges, EVPN-VPWS uses Ethernet auto-discovery route advertisements for single-homed Ethernet Segments, so upon a link or port failure of a given single-homed segment the PE must withdraw the associated per-EVPN-instance routes.

For multihomed customer edges, and for faster convergence with either single-active or all-active redundancy, a mass withdraw technique is used. A PE previously advertising a per-Ethernet-Segment auto-discovery route can withdraw this route by signalling to the remote PEs to switch all the VPWS service instances associated with that multihomed segment to the backup PE. Just as in RFC 7432, the Ethernet auto-discovery per-EVPN-instance route must not be used for traffic forwarding by a remote PE until it also receives the associated set of per-Ethernet-Segment routes.
sections.plainLanguage: When the link to the customer drops, the provider router withdraws the routes for the services on that link. For a customer connected to two routers, the segment route is withdrawn instead, which tells the far end to send everything to the surviving router.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The mechanisms in this document use the EVPN control plane as defined in RFC 7432, and the security considerations described there are equally applicable. The document uses MPLS and IP-based tunnel technologies to support data-plane transport, and the security considerations described in RFC 7432 and in the EVPN overlay work are equally applicable. The document defines no new security considerations of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is introduced: the signalling is EVPN, and the tunnels are the usual MPLS or IP tunnels, so the security rules that already apply to EVPN apply here.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has allocated the EVPN extended community sub-type 0x04 for the EVPN Layer 2 Attributes. The document also creates a registry called EVPN Layer 2 Attributes Control Flags, in which new registrations are made through the RFC Required procedure defined in RFC 8126. The initial registrations are P, for an advertising PE that is the primary PE, B, for an advertising PE that is the backup PE, and C, for a control word that must be present.
sections.plainLanguage: One new extended community number is reserved for these attributes, and the three flag bits inside it are registered so that everyone uses the same names for them.

items.label: Primary

items.desc: A control word must be present when sending EVPN packets to this PE.

viz.caption: The service interfaces used by EVPN-VPWS

items.title: VLAN-based
items.text: One VLAN on one interface maps to one service instance. The VLAN ID may differ at the two ends, and the disposition PE translates it.

items.title: VLAN bundle
items.text: A group of VLANs on one interface maps to one service instance. Each VLAN has a single ID and no translation is allowed.

items.title: Port-based
items.text: A special case of the VLAN bundle, where every VLAN on the port maps to the same service instance.
